title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 214: Beyond the Double Helix: Epigenetics
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 214 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

Beyond the Double Helix: The Epigenetics Revolution

Paragraph 1. Ever since James Watson and Francis Crick described the double-helix shape of DNA in 1953, biology was dominated by genetic determinism. Scientists widely believed that a person's DNA code acted as an unchangeable blueprint set at birth. Under this old model, your future risks for illness, ageing, and physical strength appeared completely fixed by the genes inherited from your parents.

Paragraph 2. In recent decades, however, a field called epigenetics has overturned that strict view. Epigenetics studies functional shifts in gene activity that happen without changing the basic DNA sequence itself. Think of the human body as a computer system: while the DNA hardware remains identical inside every cell, epigenetic markers work like software that instructs each cell when to turn specific genetic programs on or off.

Paragraph 3. Cells control gene activity mainly through two chemical tools. In DNA methylation, tiny methyl clusters attach directly to spots along the DNA strand, blocking cell machinery from reading the gene and switching it off. In a second method, long DNA threads wind tightly around barrel-shaped proteins called histones. When chemical tags loosen these spools, genes become active; when tags squeeze histones tightly together, genes stay silent.

Paragraph 4. Crucially, lifestyle and environmental conditions constantly reshape these switches. Stress, pollution, exercise, and food choices all modify methyl tags. Biologist Dr. Moshe Szyf tested this in laboratory rodents: baby rats ignored by their mothers developed heavy methyl blocks on stress-control genes and grew into fearful adults. When scientists later gave those animals medicine to strip away the extra methyl tags, their calm behaviour returned. Even more surprisingly, studies of the 1944 Dutch Hunger Winter showed that severe starvation during pregnancy altered metabolic genes in both children and grandchildren.

Paragraph 5. These findings are creating hopeful new medical treatments. Unlike fixed genetic errors that require difficult gene-editing surgery, epigenetic tags are chemically reversible. Cancer specialists have developed drugs that remove unwanted methyl locks from protective tumor-fighting genes, stopping bone marrow cancer growth while leaving healthy cells undamaged.
